routes.description: Establish that objective moral values and duties require a transcendent personal ground, identify God's nature and authority as that ground, and show why evolutionary or material descriptions cannot supply binding normativity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects moral objectivity, obligation, and purpose to an invariant personal source while answering the principal naturalistic, arbitrariness, and moral-knowledge alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that God, understood as the personal ground of goodness and obligation, explains objective morality more completely than science, evolution, and human flourishing alone.

centralBridges.description: Establish that objective moral comparison, binding duties, and human purpose require a standard, authority, and telos beyond individual or social opinion.
Explain why empirical and evolutionary accounts of behavior do not by themselves generate prescriptive duties or an objective hierarchy among competing moral dispositions.
Defend God's nature as the nonarbitrary moral standard rather than locating goodness outside God or in contingent commands.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect trustworthy reasoning, freedom, and moral agency to a conception of persons not exhausted by blind material processes.
Distinguish questions about knowing or interpreting moral truths from the ontological question of what makes those truths objective.

routes.description: Establish an objective moral framework centered on sentient interests, autonomy, liberty, and flourishing; explain its evolutionary and empirical basis; and challenge the necessity and reliability of divine grounding.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if evolved moral capacities and reasoned attention to individual welfare support objective moral judgment while divine-command, scriptural, and theistic accounts face unresolved explanatory or epistemic objections.

motionBridge.description: Show that science, evolution, and principles of sentient flourishing can explain objective moral capacities and judgments without requiring a supernatural personal ground.

centralBridges.description: Account for empathy, fairness, reciprocity, and cooperation as evolved capacities that make moral understanding and social life possible.
Specify survival, flourishing, autonomy, liberty, and equal consideration as standards for judging conduct and constraining aggregate welfare.
Show why rival revelations, interpretive disagreement, historical revision, or contingent commands impede a reliable divine or scriptural moral method.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain moral progress through widening equal consideration, reform led by affected persons, and correction through evidence and reason.
Test whether suffering and the history of religious moral practice cohere with a perfectly good divine moral ground.

sections.title: The Ground of Objective Standards and Duties
sections.rationale: This section addresses the motion's primary ontological burden: whether objective moral standards and binding obligations require a personal divine source or can exist within a naturalistic account.

sections.title: Evolution, Flourishing, and the Is–Ought Bridge
sections.rationale: This section tests whether evolved capacities, cooperation, sentient welfare, autonomy, and flourishing can support prescriptive moral judgments rather than merely describe behavior and survival.

sections.title: Divine Authority, Revelation, and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: This section covers the relationship between moral grounding and moral access, including divine-command arbitrariness, scriptural interpretation, religious diversity, and the distinction between ontology and epistemology.

sections.title: Reason, Agency, and the Nature of Persons
sections.rationale: This section examines whether material and evolutionary processes can sustain trustworthy reasoning and responsible moral agency, or whether those capacities require an immaterial or theistic basis.

sections.title: Moral Progress, Rights, and Difficult Applications
sections.rationale: This section tests each framework through historical reform and contested cases involving equal rights, liberty, suffering, and conflicts between individual autonomy and collective welfare.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Objective moral rules require a standard beyond human opinion, an authoritative personal rule-giver, and an objective purpose for human life.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage continues Turek's uninterrupted opening statement and repeatedly presents the analogy as his own illustration.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly states the pro route's standard, authority, and purpose requirements; no earlier opposing target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly develops all three announced components of its constructive claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three requirements are recoverable and stable, though the claimed necessity is only implicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogies motivate the requirements but do not establish that each is necessary for objective morality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The components fit together, but the move leaves a material bridge from rules to a personal rule-giver and telos.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The case rests mainly on the game and map analogies without defending their applicability to morality.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the motion bridge's asserted personal ground and transcendent standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is examined within this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly requires a transcendent standard, authoritative person, and purpose beyond human opinion.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Comparative moral judgments presuppose a standard beyond the persons or societies being compared, and God's nature supplies that external moral standard.
moves.attributionBasis: This is a continuous first-person segment of Turek's opening statement, with no speaker transition or attributed competing speech.

response.rationale: This constructive move offers comparative moral judgment and God's nature as the pro route's grounding explanation; no target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly connects the comparison analogy to the proposed divine standard.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable, but external standard shifts from a comparison referent to God's nature without full explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A standard beyond compared persons is plausible, but identifying that standard specifically with God remains underwarranted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparison inference is usable, but the bridge from an external criterion to God's nature is materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Mother Teresa, Hitler, and map comparisons illustrate the claim but do not independently establish divine grounding.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the motion-level claim that God's nature grounds objective comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span advances its own analogy without treating a developed alternative account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares maps, Mother Teresa, and Hitler, then identifies God's nature as the standard.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Evolution describes what happens but lacks the personal authority required to prescribe binding duties about how people ought to behave.
moves.attributionBasis: Turek remains the sole speaker and explicitly advances the fortune-cookie and legal-authority illustrations in his opening case.

response.rationale: This constructive move develops the central is–ought and authority objection to evolution; it has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly distinguishes evolutionary description from authoritative moral prescription.

precisionFindings.rationale: The descriptive-prescriptive distinction is clear, with the personal-authority premise left as an implicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The is–ought challenge is well identified, but only personal authority can supply duties is asserted rather than shown.

charity.alternative: Evolution may inform morality without itself being treated as a commanding person.
charity.decisiveQualification: An empirical account still needs a normative bridge explaining binding duties.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The descriptive-prescriptive distinction is coherent, with one bounded unsupported bridge to personal authority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The genetic-code example supports the category distinction, but the exclusive authority claim lacks alternative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the indispensable pro is–ought bridge at the top of the central tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly isolates descriptive evolution, though it compresses naturalistic accounts that add independent normative premises.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says evolution describes what happens and a mutating genetic code lacks authority to command behavior.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Reducing persons to molecular machines undermines free will and trustworthy reasoning, including the rational capacities required for morality and science.
moves.attributionBasis: The argument occurs in Turek's uninterrupted opening statement and includes explicit contrasts between atheism, materialism, and theism.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the pro subsidiary argument connecting nonmaterial personhood to reason and agency; no target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The causal chain from material mechanism to distrust of reasoning is explicitly presented.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is recoverable, but material causation, reaction, absence of reason, and unreliability are treated as equivalent.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts that material determination eliminates reasoning and trust without addressing reliable mechanistic cognition.

charity.alternative: Material processes can realize reasoning and produce generally reliable beliefs through selection and correction.
charity.decisiveQualification: Causal determination alone does not entail absence of inference or epistemic reliability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion depends on an unsupported transition from physical causation to no reasoning and wholesale unreliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The molecular-machine characterization is asserted without evidence that physical realization defeats rational warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary reason-and-agency bridge and reaches its principal inferential requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: Calling persons mere reacting robots omits the strongest materialist distinction between causal realization and irrationality.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says molecular machines merely react, lack free will, and therefore cannot trust even atheistic thoughts.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Divine-command and scriptural approaches provide no reliable moral method when commands appear contingent, texts contain conflicting norms, and moral judgments change over time.
moves.attributionBasis: Shermer explicitly identifies Turek's position before presenting this sustained critique during his own uninterrupted opening statement.

components.text: Whether a transcendent personal authority supplies stable and communicable objective moral rules.
Whether God's nature can function as a stable external standard despite changing religious judgments.

response.rationale: Changing religious judgments and conflicting norms contact the claimed communicative authority and stability, but do not fully answer the ontological grounding claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive authority component but leaves the independent ontological-standard component unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The method objection is clear, but examples of changing believers sometimes broaden into claims about religion generally.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Historical change supports an epistemic challenge, though it cannot alone show that every divine method is unreliable.

charity.alternative: Moral truth may remain fixed even when believers misinterpret or slowly recognize it.
charity.decisiveQualification: A grounding account still needs a reliable means of identifying commands and resolving conflicting texts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The examples support an epistemic reliability challenge, though changing judgments do not entail a changing ground.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Slavery and marriage supply concrete examples, but the selected evidence does not document the broader textual-conflict claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central con bridge challenging reliable divine and scriptural moral access.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves the practical epistemic problem but underplays the distinction between truth and changing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt predicts changed religious positions and presents moral change as contrary to a fixed divine-method account.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: The survival and flourishing of individual sentient beings supplies a basis for objective morality, supported by evolved empathy, reciprocal altruism, and cooperation.
moves.attributionBasis: The entire passage is part of Shermer's uninterrupted opening statement and contains his explicit formulation of an objective moral system.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the con route's naturalistic basis in sentient flourishing and evolved social capacities; no target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies both the proposed standard and the capacities supporting it.

precisionFindings.rationale: Sentience and flourishing remain stable, while how conflicts among flourishing interests are resolved is implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move reasonably proposes a moral starting point but overstates the derivation of an objective ought from flourishing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposed foundation is intelligible, but the bridge from evolved concern to objective normative authority remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Empathy, bonding, and cooperation support moral capacity, but they do not alone warrant flourishing as objectively binding.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by proposing a naturalistic objective-morality ground.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive passage does not substantially interpret or answer an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies empathy and social bonding, then calls sentient survival and flourishing a basis for objective morals.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Moral emotions and sensitivity to justice and fairness are evolved, innate capacities observable in adults, children, primates, and capuchin monkeys.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted presentation remains in Shermer's first-person lecture voice and explains his primate experiment example.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies cross-species observations for the con evolved-capacities bridge; no response target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly identifies the capacities, their proposed origin, and the populations in which they appear.

precisionFindings.rationale: The observed capacities are clear, but innate, evolved, and genetically packaged are asserted across a broad scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Cross-species observation supports evolutionary continuity, but certainty about innateness and genetic specification needs further warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cross-species pattern coherently supports evolved capacities, with one bounded inference from observation to genetic innateness.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Adults, infants, primates, and capuchins provide representative examples, though experimental details and rival learning accounts are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central evolved-capacities bridge through empathy, fairness, and cross-species continuity.

representationalCharity.rationale: No meaningful opposing interpretation is developed in this constructive evidentiary span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls justice and fairness evolved and innate and reports their presence in adults, infants, and primates.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Science, reason, and Enlightenment humanism offer methods for correcting harmful moral and social beliefs that religious superstition has sustained.
moves.attributionBasis: Shermer explicitly labels this his final point and carries the argument continuously through the conclusion of his presentation.

components.text: Whether material and evolutionary processes can sustain trustworthy reasoning rather than mere reaction.
Whether science and reason can supply authoritative objective standards rather than only problem-solving methods.

response.rationale: The appeal to successful science and reason bears on rational practice but does not answer the causal argument that materialism allegedly undermines rational warrant.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It offers relevant contrary practice but leaves the earlier move's decisive materialism-to-unreliability inference untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed method is recoverable, but religion and superstition are generalized beyond the supplied historical illustration.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Science and reason can correct factual beliefs, but their sufficiency for resolving moral standards is asserted broadly.

charity.alternative: Religious moral reasoning can incorporate evidence and reason rather than resting solely on superstition.
charity.decisiveQualification: A reliable moral method still requires transparent correction of harmful factual and interpretive claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The corrective-method conclusion is plausible, but factual problem-solving does not by itself establish moral normativity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Enlightenment contrast is historically suggestive but selectively asserted and lacks representative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the subsidiary pro reason bridge, but only indirectly through the demonstrated practice of scientific correction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The Iron Age and superstition framing materially compresses the strongest intellectually engaged religious alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts earlier Christian superstition with Enlightenment humanism and urges science and reason for moral problems.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Genocide is wrong because collectivist extermination destroys sentient individuals' survival, flourishing, rights, and freedom from torture and suffering.
moves.attributionBasis: Shermer answers Turek directly in his established vocabulary of sentient beings, survival, flourishing, rights, and collectivism.

components.text: Whether an objective framework can explain why genocide is wrong without a transcendent personal rule-giver.
Whether comparative condemnation can rest on sentient rights rather than God's nature.

response.rationale: The move directly supplies survival, suffering, rights, and anti-collectivism as grounds for condemnation, while leaving their ultimate authority compressed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive demand and offers a concrete rival basis, but does not fully defend that basis's objectivity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The condemnation and protected interests are clear, with the extension of rights beyond humans implicitly bounded by sentience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Certainty that genocide violates the identified interests fits the direct extermination, suffering, and rights-removal rationale.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Extermination straightforwardly violates survival, bodily security, and rights, though the rights foundation remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The consequences of genocide strongly support the condemnation, but objective rights are invoked rather than independently grounded.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by applying sentient flourishing to a central test case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply supplies its own condemnation rather than interpreting an alternative in a charity-sensitive way.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grounds genocide's wrongness in extermination, removed rights, torture, suffering, and collectivism.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Moral progress occurs when oppressed people and their allies demand equal rights and societies expand autonomy despite longstanding religious resistance.
moves.attributionBasis: Shermer answers the Nazi-values question and continues through linked examples of slavery, women's suffrage, and same-sex marriage.

components.text: Whether God's nature, rather than people or societies, supplies the objective standard for moral comparison.
Whether religious authority reliably communicates and enforces objective moral rules.

response.rationale: Historical religious resistance contacts institutional reliability and moral progress, but does not answer whether God's nature could remain the ontological standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary authority component while leaving the decisive grounding inference unaddressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The progress mechanism is clear, but claims about Christians opposing reforms are stated without denominational or historical scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Affected-group agency is well illustrated, but universal claims about Christian opposition exceed the selected support.

charity.alternative: Christian actors and principles also contributed materially to abolition and other rights reforms.
charity.decisiveQualification: Substantial religious resistance can still undermine claims of uniquely reliable scriptural guidance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Oppressed-group advocacy plausibly drives progress, but religious resistance alone does not explain the full causal pattern.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several reforms are named, yet the sweeping historical attribution is selective and insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the subsidiary moral-progress bridge through affected persons, allies, and expanding equal rights.

representationalCharity.rationale: The assertion that Christians were the objectors omits the decisive mixed history of both religious resistance and reform.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt credits oppressed people and allies while attributing opposition to Christians across several reforms.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: An outsider requires evidence to distinguish rival claims about the correct God because confidence and monotheistic belief alone cannot adjudicate incompatible authorities.
moves.attributionBasis: Shermer explicitly restates his point, asks how outsiders can identify the right God, and presses Turek for supporting evidence.

components.text: Whether God's nature is the actual external moral standard rather than one asserted divine candidate.
Whether a purported personal authority can be identified reliably among incompatible religious claims.

response.rationale: The demand for evidence directly challenges identification of the authoritative God, but does not refute the conditional ontological claim about God's nature.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the epistemic authority component while leaving the decisive conditional grounding claim intact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The outsider-evidence demand and the incompatibility among claimed gods are both clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The interrogative force appropriately requests discriminating evidence rather than claiming rival gods are disproven.

charity.alternative: A cumulative philosophical and historical case might distinguish one conception of God from rivals.
charity.decisiveQualification: That evidence must be supplied rather than replaced by confidence or monotheistic agreement.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The outsider cannot choose among incompatible authorities from shared confidence alone; discriminating evidence is logically required.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The existence of rival Muslim and Christian claims supports the demand, though their detailed evidential cases are not compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central divine-epistemic bridge by demanding a reliable discriminator among rival revelations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge leaves open evidential adjudication and accurately focuses on the need to discriminate incompatible authorities.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how outsiders can identify the right God and repeatedly requests evidence beyond asserted belief.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Biblical slavery differed from race-based chattel slavery, condemned slave trading, affirmed equal human dignity, and contained principles directed toward liberation.
moves.attributionBasis: Turek gives an enumerated answer after requesting his presentation slide, and Shermer resumes the challenge only on the next row.

components.text: Whether Christianity uniformly resisted abolition and therefore exemplifies unreliable religious moral guidance.
Whether biblical texts contain slavery norms that undermine a stable divine moral method.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes forms of slavery and cites anti-trading and equality principles, though it does not resolve every coercive biblical practice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both historical and textual components but leaves important coercion and implementation qualifications unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinctions are recoverable, but Old Testament slavery is generalized as voluntary despite the acknowledged captive category.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Some distinctions are relevant, but the categorical description of biblical slavery exceeds the selected evidence and its own exceptions.

charity.alternative: Biblical slavery included debt service alongside coercive captive and inherited forms unlike modern race slavery.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting race-based chattel slavery does not by itself answer the moral status of other coercive ownership.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Condemnation of trading and equal dignity support reform, but do not entail that all permitted slavery was voluntary or liberating.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several textual propositions are asserted without representative passages or treatment of counterexamples within biblical law.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary con moral-progress bridge through the slavery example and biblical principles.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies real distinctions but materially underrepresents the strongest objection concerning non-racial coercive servitude.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes debt service and captives from racial slavery and invokes anti-trading and equal-dignity teachings.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Disputes about interpreting and knowing moral rules are epistemic questions distinct from the prior ontological question of what grounds objective moral laws.
moves.attributionBasis: Turek explicitly distinguishes metaphysics from epistemology and illustrates ordinary interpretive principles with familiar metaphors.

components.text: Whether difficulty identifying the correct God defeats the ontological claim that God grounds objective morality.
Whether interpretive disagreement concerns moral truth's ground or access to that truth.

response.rationale: The reply expressly distinguishes grounding from knowledge and interpretation, but it does not satisfy the con route's independent demand for reliable access.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive inference and limits its consequence, while leaving the legitimate epistemic challenge unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: Ontology, epistemology, linguistics, and hermeneutics are consistently distinguished and their relationship is expressly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that access and grounding are distinct is well matched to the conceptual distinction offered.

charity.alternative: The con challenge targets reliable divine moral methodology, not merely the existence of a metaphysical ground.
charity.decisiveQualification: An epistemic failure need not refute ontology but can still impair the route's explanatory completeness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between what grounds a truth and how it is known is explicit, valid, and consistently illustrated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary interpretation provides relevant support, though it does not establish that difficult revelations are reliably interpretable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the subsidiary pro knowledge-grounding bridge at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The distinction is fair and important, though calling the issue a step removed understates its independent route significance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly contrasts where objective moral laws come from with linguistics, hermeneutics, and ordinary interpretation.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.proposition: Individual autonomy, liberty, and bodily integrity can override aggregate welfare, as shown by the impermissibility of killing one healthy person to save five others.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives the floor to Michael Shermer, and the sustained answer is delivered in his first-person argumentative voice.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies autonomy and bodily integrity as constraints on aggregate flourishing; no earlier target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The transplant case clearly states the conflict, judgment, and autonomy-based constraint.

precisionFindings.rationale: The constraint is clear, though the conditions under which autonomy overrides welfare remain implicitly rather than exhaustively bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical judgment in the involuntary organ-harvesting case fits the clearly specified violation of bodily autonomy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The case coherently demonstrates that aggregate benefit is constrained by individual bodily rights and liberty.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The transplant example is probative, though the phrase that society decided the rule leaves its objective status underexplained.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central flourishing-rights bridge by specifying a constraint on aggregate welfare.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops a hard case without engaging a live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects killing one healthy person for five organs because individual sanctity, autonomy, and liberty override group gain.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Hard moral dilemmas presuppose that human lives possess objective value, supporting the existence of objective moral law and a moral lawgiver.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Frank Turek's response, and the ensuing argument directly contrasts his position with Michael Shermer's example.

components.text: Whether the transplant dilemma demonstrates objective individual value and a principled constraint on welfare.
Whether an evolutionary worldview can recognize human value and morally significant dilemmas.

response.rationale: The reply directly interprets the dilemma as evidence of objective value, but its move from value to a divine lawgiver and its naturalist caricature remain unsupported.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive example and value premise, while failing to answer the autonomy principle on its own terms.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is recoverable, but objective value, objective law, and divine lawgiver are moved between without stable bridging.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A recognized dilemma does not by itself necessitate a divine lawgiver, and the naturalistic alternative is dismissed categorically.

charity.alternative: Evolutionary naturalists can value sentient lives and defend autonomy without treating people as disposable germs.
charity.decisiveQualification: Recognizing value does not settle whether its ground is naturalistic, nonnatural, or divine.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from a hard dilemma to objective value is plausible, but the further necessity of a lawgiver is a non sequitur.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The transplant dilemma supports perceived value, while the claims about evolutionary indifference and divine grounding lack support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con flourishing-rights bridge through the autonomy dilemma's asserted grounding.

representationalCharity.rationale: The claim that an evolutionary worldview would push everyone treats a live rights-based alternative as if it had no values.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the dilemma presupposes valuable life, caricatures evolutionary indifference, and infers a moral lawgiver.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Evolution and material processes describe what survives but cannot prescribe what ought to survive or impose binding duties to cooperate rather than exploit.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted closing statement uses Turek's characteristic first-person references to Michael and develops the pro side's naturalism critique.

components.text: Whether survival and flourishing can generate objective prescriptions rather than merely identify evolved outcomes.
Whether evolved cooperation has normative priority over evolved exploitation or violence.
Whether autonomy supplies an independent normative constraint beyond descriptive survival.

response.rationale: The move directly presses the is–ought and selection-among-dispositions objections, but it does not address autonomy as an independent normative premise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive flourishing-ground component and a second evolutionary component, leaving the autonomy constraint unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The descriptive-prescriptive distinction and questions about which beings and behaviors ought to survive are expressly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The is–ought objection is strong against bare evolution, but the move assumes the con case contains no independent normative premises.

charity.alternative: The con framework adds sentient interests, equal consideration, and autonomy rather than deriving duties from survival alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those added standards still require a defended account of objective normative authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The challenge correctly distinguishes what survives from what ought to survive, with a bounded overreach against richer premises.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Contrasting cooperation, exploitation, and Nazi survival concretely exposes underdetermination, though rival normative premises are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con motion bridge by challenging the prescriptive sufficiency of evolution and flourishing.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies the decisive bridge problem but repeatedly reduces the richer flourishing account to survival alone.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the move from material evolution to moral law a category mistake and asks why some survival strategies ought to prevail.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Minds, logical laws, moral values, love, and justice are immaterial realities that cannot be reduced to matter, so persons are more than physical machines.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted closing statement remains in Turek's voice and explicitly opposes Michael's materialism while advancing a soul-body distinction.

components.text: Whether science and reason provide practical methods for correcting harmful moral beliefs.
Whether evolved physical organisms can instantiate moral cognition and fairness.

response.rationale: The immateriality claim bears on physical realization of moral cognition but does not answer whether scientific reasoning functions as a corrective method.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary physical-realization issue while leaving the primary methodological demand unaddressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: Immaterial alternates between abstract propositions, descriptive laws, mental states, and values as though they shared one ontology.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Nonphysical description or abstractness does not establish causal substance dualism or the irreducibility of persons.

charity.alternative: Abstract truths can be nonmaterial while minds and moral cognition are physically realized.
charity.decisiveQualification: Irreducibility of propositions does not entail an immaterial personal substance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion that persons exceed matter does not follow from grouping abstract laws, values, and mental phenomena as immaterial.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Gravity's law and moral concepts are illustrative, but no warrant connects their abstract status to a nonphysical mind.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary pro reason-and-agency bridge through an asserted irreducibility of mind.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move groups distinct categories together and omits the strongest physicalist distinction between representation and represented truth.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt groups minds, logical and natural laws, morality, love, and justice as realities unexplained by molecules.

moves.speaker: Frank Turek
moves.proposition: Goodness is neither external to God nor arbitrarily invented by divine command because God's unchanging nature is itself the objective moral standard.
moves.attributionBasis: Turek explicitly identifies Michael's earlier Euthyphro challenge and answers both alternatives during his uninterrupted closing statement.

components.text: Whether divine morality must be external to God or arbitrarily created by contingent commands.
Whether identifying God's nature as the standard distinguishes the correct divine claimant.

response.rationale: The reply expressly rejects both Euthyphro horns by locating the standard in God's unchanging nature, but it does not answer the rival-gods evidence demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly diagnoses the dilemma's assumed alternatives and states the proposed defeating third account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two horns and the proposed divine-nature alternative are clearly and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The third-option response defeats the stated dichotomy, though it does not independently prove that divine nature is good.

charity.alternative: Even if goodness is God's nature, one may ask whether calling that nature good is substantive or stipulative.
charity.decisiveQualification: The divine-nature account avoids arbitrary commands but still needs an explanatory account of goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Locating goodness in an unchanging nature is a coherent third option, with one bounded explanatory circularity concern.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual answer is clearly stated, but God's nature and its necessary goodness are asserted rather than defended.

components.text: Whether matter and evolutionary history can produce beings capable of genuine moral knowledge and wisdom.

Whether material embodiment itself supplies binding moral authority.
